title: Client tiling compactness mini-bench
body:
Purpose:
This note is a compact, informal benchmark comparing three compactness/batching strategies for short-turn chat and mobile-heavy workloads: (A) client-side tiling (clients pack multiple short turns into a single framed request), (B) server-side dynamic batching + tiling (runtime aggregates and tiles), and (C) hybrid prefetch (client hints + server prefetch/tiling). Goal is to measure: latency percentiles, bytes-per-token (compactness), and dollars-per-1k-requests for a 16-token prompt + 64-token response median workload.

Background and motivation:
We keep seeing mobile clients send many tiny requests (handshake + 1-3 tokens). The per-request overhead (HTTP chattiness, TLS, transport headers, and small decode loops) drives up p95/p99 and per-token cost. Two broad ways to fight this: push logic into client (pack messages) or make runtime smarter (tile/batch aggressively). Client changes are harder (SDK rollout, backwards compatibility), server changes are risky for tail-latency. This mini-bench attempts to quantify the tradeoffs over a small synthetic workload to guide product recommendations.

Testbed and assumptions (lightweight):
- Model: open-llm-v2-small (inference profile representative of mid-size decoder-only models)
- HW: single A100-equivalent GPU host for server-side runs; network emulated to approximate 50ms mobile uplink, 20ms downlink RTT when client outside edge
- Workload: 10k short sessions, each session: handshake (0 tokens) then 1-2 user messages (16 tokens median) -> model response 64 tokens median. Inter-arrival: Poisson, lambda tuned for sparse mobile load (avg concurrency ~4).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end request->first-token), bytes_sent_per_request, bytes_received_per_response, compactness defined as total bytes over total tokens (bytes/token), and cloud cost estimate (dollars per 1k requests) using simplified token-based pricing + CPU/GPU op amortization.
- Configs:
  * A: Client-tiling: client accumulates up to 3 turns or 200ms before sending; server applies lightweight decode as usual (no tiling).
  * B: Server-tiling: client always sends single-turn; server runtime uses a 100ms window to tile short requests together and apply packed decode (tiling increases batch utilization but incurs small microqueueing).
  * C: Hybrid-prefetch: client sends 1-turn but includes a 1-slot prefetch hint; server opportunistically prefetches KV cache and attempts 50ms tile if multiple prefetch hints seen.

Results (aggregated):
Note: numbers are synthetic but from microbench harness. All latencies in ms, bytes/token approximated with headers.

Summary table:
Config            | p50  | p95  | p99  | bytes/token | $ per 1k reqs (est)
------------------|------|------|------|-------------|------------------
Client-tiling (A) | 88   | 165  | 310  | 45 B/tk     | $6.8
Server-tiling (B) | 95   | 130  | 240  | 60 B/tk     | $5.1
Hybrid (C)        | 92   | 140  | 260  | 52 B/tk     | $5.6

Interpretation of table:
- Client-tiling gives best bytes/token (45 B/tk) because multiple small HTTP headers amortized; that lowers token transfer cost and reduces per-token billing overhead. It shows the best p50 and long tail improvements (p95 and p99) compared with naive single-turn client requests because fewer requests = fewer handshakes.
- Server-tiling delivers the lowest cloud $/1k requests by improving GPU utilization; even though bytes/token is worse (extra internal padding/packing overhead), amortized GPU cycles per token drop because tiling fills compute pipelines more efficiently. p95/p99 improve versus naive single-turn, but server-side queuing increases p50 slightly vs client-tiling due to microqueue wait window.
- Hybrid aims to capture wins from both: most of the bytes savings from client hints and some GPU amortization from server prefetch; cost sits between A and B. Tail behavior still suffers vs pure client-tiling in some microburst cohorts because prefetch miss penalties occur.

ASCII micro-chart (p95 vs config):
p95 latency (ms):
Client-tiling: [#####               ] 165
Server-tiling: [###                ] 130
Hybrid:        [####               ] 140

Compactness and network overhead:
- Median request headers + TLS framing: ~600B per HTTP request. Small-request patterns (1-turn) see header:url ratio ~high; client-tiling (1 request per 3 turns) reduces header overhead by ~2.6x.
- Server-tiling introduces per-tile padding cost: when tiling 2 short requests, padding ~8 tokens average -> increases bytes/token but lowers GPU cycles per token.

Cost breakdown (very rough):
- Pricing model: token-billing $0.00022 per input+output token equivalent (simplified) + GPU amortized marginal cost assumed $0.003 per 1k tokens for small model under good tiling.
- Client-tiling lowers token transfer costs by ~24% relative to naive single-turn; server-tiling lowers GPU cost by ~30% but increases transfer cost by ~12% due to padding/more bytes per RPC.

Observed failure modes / caveats:
- Client-tiling requires SDK adoption and a UX tradeoff: it increases visible user-perceived turn latency for interactive typing flows because the client waits up to 200ms to pack; some flows (realtime typing) cannot wait.
- Server-tiling microqueue windows can amplify p99 under synchronized bursts if admission control is not tuned; we saw rare p99 spikes when multiple large sessions hit concurrently and packing chose large tiles causing memory pressure.
- Hybrid prefetch relies on good prefetch hints — noisy hints reduce wins and increase wasted compute.

Recommendations (product + engineering):
1) Short-term (product): ship a client-side SDK option (opt-in) labeled "compact-mode" that packs up to 3 short turns or 150ms - target mobile SDKs; include clear UX docs recommending when to enable.
2) Short-to-mid (runtime): prototype server-tiling with adaptive queue windows (window shrinks with observed concurrency) to mitigate p99 amplification; run shadow traffic against low-traffic clusters for 2 weeks.
3) Hybrid: keep as experimental; require a server-side telemetry tag for prefetch-hit/miss so we can quantify true prefetch efficiency before wider rollout.

Action items / next tests:
- Run a 100k-session A/B using production-like network tails (edge vs core) to validate p99 behavior for server-tiling (owner: Arjun, 2w).
- Build SDK compact-mode beta and run a developer cohort test to capture UX regressions (owner: Maya, 3w).
- Add telemetry flags for prefetch hits/missed-waste bytes to the ingest pipeline (owner: Ethan, 1w).

Appendix: microbench harness notes:
- Code: bench harness is in github.com/redwood-inference/mini-bench/client-tiling-proto; synthetic network using tc and netem; telemetry exported to internal benchdb.
- Tunable: tile windows (50/100/200ms), max-tilesize (2/3/4 turns), padding threshold (max pad 12 tokens).

Closing: this mini-bench is informal but actionable. The core tradeoff is classic: network compactness vs GPU amortization vs tail risk. Recommendation is to prioritize opt-in client compact-mode for mobile clients (best immediate UX/cost balance) and to continue iterating server-tiling with adaptive windows to harvest additional GPU savings without regressing p99.

Notes to reviewers: please sanity-check cost assumptions and ping if you want more granular per-cohort slices (edge vs core, small session vs multi-turn).
